site.name: Chrysolite Mine
site.componentDetail: Historic Fryer Hill silver-lead carbonate mine
overview: Chrysolite was one of the famous Fryer Hill mines that helped define Leadville’s late-1870s silver boom. Government mining reports place it among the important carbonate-ore workings on Fryer Hill, where rich lead-silver deposits were developed beneath a complex sequence of porphyry, limestone, and quartzite.
The mine is historically tied to Horace Tabor’s rise during the Leadville boom, but Remnant treats Chrysolite as its own mine rather than as an extension of nearby properties.

timeline.text: Chrysolite emerged during the first rush of major carbonate discoveries on Fryer Hill as Leadville’s silver boom accelerated.
The mine became one of the significant Fryer Hill producers documented in federal mining reports and detailed geological mapping.
Leadville mining continued through changing metal markets; government accounts record work on Chrysolite dumps as operators sought value from previously mined material.
Federal geological work documented the Chrysolite workings in detail, including shaft areas and the complicated Fryer Hill ore geology.

moreHistory: Fryer Hill was one of the most intensely developed parts of the Leadville district. Chrysolite worked the same broad carbonate-ore environment that made neighboring mines famous, but each property followed its own shafts, stopes, faults, and ore bodies.

Historic federal mapping documents Chrysolite mine workings and later shaft development, making the mine useful for understanding how Leadville operators chased ore through a difficult three-dimensional geologic setting.
